I'm Terry Schmidt, general manager of transportation and construction.
On an annual basis, administration presents a report requesting council approval of the current year adjusted and next year preliminary prepaid servicing rates.

Administration has reviewed the actual 2024 costs of land developed by the city as well as the 2025 tenders received and any change in standards in order to establish the proposed adjustment to 2025 offsite and direct services and set the preliminary rates for 2026.
The city does not allocate general revenues to be used for funding infrastructure for land development.
The financial source of revenue for construction of infrastructure for land development to new areas within the city is the prepaid service rates.

The prepaid rates are divided into two major servicing categories, direct services which benefit the frontage of the property and offsite services which benefit the neighborhood or catchment area as a whole.

The proposed rates in this report were discussed and received by Saskatoon land, corporate financial services department, as well as with members of the developers liaison committee from the Saskatoon region homebuilders association that utilize these rates.
The proposed rate increases are required to generate the revenue needed to meet projected and actual expenditures for cost recovery of the provided services.
All land development tenders have been issued and the cost analysis of these tenders including information on construction costs from the past year are the main source for the prepaid service rates.
Global inflation surged after 2020 due to pandemic related supply chain bottlenecks and geopolitical tensions.
During these years, annual rate increases of 2.9% 5.5% and a 5.5% were recognized in 2021, 2022 and 23 respectively.
Last year, city council approved a 2.3% increase to residential offsite services rates as contract, unipricing and other indexes were trending lower and appear to be stabilizing.

However, this year, the construction industry is still facing higher costs and economic uncertainties with international trade imports, tariff wars and specifically tariffs imposed on steel and aluminum products.
Energy and petroleum prices, non-theres metal products, cement and fabricated construction materials have still experienced pricing increasing ranging from 4% to 26%.

These component cost changes have been verified across Canada by average statistics candidate industry price indexes over the last year and noticed within unit pricing of recent contract tenders and quotations.

The city continues to develop prepaid service rates that see stability and would like to emphasize that the city's rates generally absorb significant cost changes by smoothing these increases gradually over time.
The overall proposed prepaid service rate for the recovery of cost for residential property would increase by 2.5% for offsite services and 3.1% for direct services for combined increase of 2.9%.

The overall proposed prepaid service rates recovery of cost for institutional commercial and school property would increase by 2.3% for offsite services and 3.2% for direct services for combined increase of 2.9%.
The overall proposed prepaid rates for the recovery of cost for industrial property would increase by 2% for offsite services and 3% for direct services for combined increase of 2.6%.
The prepaid rate changes by zoning area are attached in appendix 1 and appendix 2 provides details on the prepaid service rate evaluations.

The proposed changes for administration of the line development program to account for changes in standard collective agreements and car allowance rates is between 2.3% and 3.7% compared to between 2.6% and 3.7% in 2024.
The purpose of adjusting the prepaid rates is to recover the cost of providing prepaid services for the preparation of service lots for sale in Saskatoon.

Director of Recreation and Community Development. This report which occurs annually seeks approval
for the 2025 rate for the Parks and Recreation Lovey, the Elementary School Land Lovey,
and the High School Land Lovey. By resolution, city council establishes levies to fund the
development of parks and community amenities and the purchase of land for future school sites.
Administration is recommending an increase of 4.37% to the 2025 Parks and Recreation Lovey
based on an average increase in park design and construction costs of 4.82%.
Increased funding required for future parks satellite maintenance buildings and a partial offset
by interest received on funds that are held in the Parks and Recreation Lovey accounts.
The Elementary School Land Lovey, which funds the year to year cost of acquiring land for
future elementary schools, for that lovey administration is recommending an increase of 13%
directly tied to the increase in land costs. The preliminary high school land
Lovey which was approved by city council in May of 2024 to begin in 2025, administration is recommending
a decrease of 5.6% due to projected land costs, interest occurred in the account,
and an increase in the average neighborhood front meters from 35,000 to 37,000.
levies are collected at the time of servicing of lots, so lots that are service prior to 2025
would not be subject to these new rates. All lots serviced after January 1, 2025,
as well as all future lots citywide would be subject to these new levy rates if approved.
In 2025, following a written request from Mayor Block to the Minister of Education,
a school site working group was convened. The group consisted of representatives from the city's
administration, the province, city of Regina, developers from both cities, the Saskatchewan
Association of Rural Municipalities, and Saskatchewan Urban Municipalities Association.
Several meetings were held with discussions focused on the Planning and Development Act,
funding mechanisms for school lands, and collaborative future planning between all levels of
government. Several recommendations were developed and provided to the province by the respective
groups in the summer of 2025. The government of Saskatchewan has indicated its intent.
to introduce new legislation to address the school land issue.
On November 13th of 2025, the Minister of Education moved 1st reading of Bill number 38,
the Building Schools Faster Act, and Act of Respecting Land Acquisition of Renew Schools,
and making related amendments to the Planning and Development Act.
Some key clauses in Bill 38 that are that applies to new schools only.
Cities continue to be responsible for planning and acquiring service land that meets
requirements for the building of new schools, and before acquiring land for new
school, the city will enter into a contribution agreement with the province.
This agreement will include terms and conditions on a cost sharing formula and a cost
contribution grant to be made by the province.
Any future contribution by the province to support the acquisition of land for future
schools would have the impact of reducing our existing school land levies with all
other things being equal.
Consequential amendments to the Education Act will also be required in conjunction with
the new act in regulations, which will be brought forward by Royal Assent.
The cost contribution formula from the province will be developed as part of those regulations.
Administration will report back to City Council in 2026 on the implications of this proposed act.
The bill is scheduled to be released past when the spring sitting of the legislative assembly
ends in mid May 2026.
The act will not come into force until regulations are passed by the cabinet.
As such, the recommendations included in this report are relevant to 2025 levies and are
based on the current state and expected future capital costs and commitments for acquiring
lands for schools by the city.
